nameStory: Little mouse-ear gets its charming name from its tiny, fuzzy leaves that really do look like the soft, rounded ears of a small mouse! The scientific name 'semidecandrum' means 'half ten stamens,' referring to the fact that this little plant typically has five stamens instead of the full ten that some of its relatives display.
description: Little mouse-ear is a tiny annual wildflower that most people walk right past without noticing. This diminutive member of the pink family grows only 2-6 inches tall, forming small clusters of fuzzy, gray-green leaves close to the ground. Its miniature white flowers are barely a quarter-inch across, with five deeply notched petals that make each bloom look like it has ten tiny petals instead of five.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers less than ¼ inch across with five deeply split petals that create a 10-petaled appearance; petals are shorter than the green sepals beneath them

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves covered in soft, silvery hairs that feel velvety to the touch; arranged in opposite pairs and clustered near the base of the plant

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing annual that forms small mats or patches, rarely exceeding 6 inches tall; stems are also covered in fine, soft hairs

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, cylindrical capsules that curve upward and split at the tip to release tiny brown seeds; capsules are longer than the flower petals

habitat: Little mouse-ear thrives in disturbed, sandy soils and open areas throughout New England, particularly favoring coastal areas, old fields, and sandy roadsides. You'll most often spot it in well-drained, somewhat poor soils where larger plants haven't taken over. It's especially common in areas with thin soil over bedrock or in sandy coastal plains.

seasonality.spring: Flowers appear in early to mid-spring (April-May) when the tiny white blooms are most visible against the small rosettes of fuzzy leaves.
seasonality.summer: Plants complete their lifecycle quickly, with seeds forming by early summer; mature plants begin to dry out and become less noticeable.
seasonality.fall: Annual plants have typically died back, leaving only seeds to overwinter in the soil.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence; exists only as seeds waiting for spring germination.

funFact: Despite being called 'little mouse-ear,' this plant is so tiny that its entire flower is smaller than the actual ear of most mice - making it more like 'baby mouse-ear' in real-world scale!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other mouse-ear chickweeds, but little mouse-ear is distinguished by being an annual (not perennial) and having petals that are shorter than the sepals - in most other mouse-ears, the petals are longer than the sepals. Remember: 'Little mouse-ear has little petals!'
contextualKnowledge: The term 'chickweed' doesn't mean these plants are related to chickens - it comes from the fact that chickens and other birds love to eat the seeds and tender leaves of plants in this group. Many mouse-ear species are non-native to New England, having arrived from Europe.
compareHints: Little mouse-ear is smaller and more delicate than common mouse-ear chickweed, which is perennial and has longer petals. Unlike the showy snow-in-summer with its bright white flowers, little mouse-ear has tiny, inconspicuous blooms. It's also much smaller than field chickweed and lacks the sticky feel of sticky mouse-ear chickweed.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its mouse-ear chickweed relatives, common mouse-ear chickweed is the most widespread and persistent in New England.
Snow-in-summer stands out dramatically from its mouse-ear chickweed relatives due to its distinctive 'tomentose' or felty white hairs covering the entire plant, giving it a silvery appearance.
Field chickweed stands out from its mouse-ear relatives by forming the densest, most mat-like growth habit and having the most deeply notched flower petals.
Among the mouse-ear chickweeds in New England, sticky mouse-ear is the only one with that distinctive clammy, tacky feel from its glandular hairs.
American field chickweed differs from other Cerastium species by having the most deeply divided petals - they're split nearly to the base.
Among the mouse-ear chickweeds in New England, common mouse-ear chickweed is the most widespread and has the most consistently fuzzy texture throughout the plant.
Unlike the very common mouse-ear chickweed which has fuzzy, spoon-shaped leaves and upright flowers, nodding chickweed has narrower leaves and distinctively drooping flowers.
Among its mouse-ear relatives, dwarf mouse-ear stands out for being the tiniest and having petals that don't extend beyond the sepals.
